def: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted from one form to another; the change in internal energy equals heat added plus work done on the system.
points: ΔU = q + w, where ΔU is change in internal energy, q is heat absorbed, w is work done on the system.
Sign convention: heat absorbed by system is +q, heat released is -q; work done ON the system is +w, work done BY the system is -w.
For an isolated system, no heat or work exchange occurs, so ΔU = 0.
At constant volume, work done = 0 (no expansion/compression), so ΔU = q (heat at constant volume = qv).
At constant pressure, work w = -PΔV (expansion work), and q at constant pressure defines enthalpy change ΔH.
Internal energy is a state function — it depends only on the initial and final states, not the path taken.
formula: ΔU = q + w     w = -P ΔV (constant pressure)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Heat q added"] --> C["Change in internal energy"]
  B["Work w done on system"] --> C
  C --> D["Delta U = q + w"]

example: A gas absorbs 500 J heat and does 200 J work on surroundings (expansion): ΔU = q + w = 500 + (-200) = 300 J.
tip: Clearly state the sign convention you are using before substituting values — many marks are lost due to sign confusion.

def: Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat absorbed or released by a system during a process at constant pressure.
points: ΔH = ΔU + PΔV (relates enthalpy change to internal energy change at constant pressure).
Enthalpy of formation: heat change when 1 mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states.
Enthalpy of combustion: heat released when 1 mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen.
Enthalpy of reaction: heat change when reactants (in stoichiometric amounts) convert completely to products.
Exothermic reactions have ΔH negative (heat released); endothermic reactions have ΔH positive (heat absorbed).
Standard enthalpy changes are measured at 298 K and 1 bar pressure, denoted ΔH°.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Reactants"] --> B{"Delta H"}
  B -->|Negative exothermic| C["Heat released"]
  B -->|Positive endothermic| D["Heat absorbed"]

example: Combustion of methane: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, ΔH = -890 kJ/mol (exothermic, heat is released).
tip: Clearly state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic based on the sign of ΔH — examiners often ask this as a follow-up.

def: Hess's law of constant heat summation states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several steps, since enthalpy is a state function.
points: Enthalpy change depends only on initial and final states, not on the path/number of steps taken.
Thermochemical equations can be added, subtracted or multiplied like algebraic equations, and their ΔH values are treated the same way.
To find ΔH of an unknown reaction, combine known reactions so that their sum gives the target reaction.
If a reaction is reversed, the sign of ΔH is also reversed.
If a reaction is multiplied by a factor, ΔH is multiplied by the same factor.
Hess's law allows calculation of enthalpies that are difficult to measure directly (e.g. enthalpy of formation of unstable compounds).
formula: ΔH(overall) = ΔH1 + ΔH2 + ... (for steps that sum to overall reaction)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Reactants"] -->|Step 1 dH1| B["Intermediate"]
  B -->|Step 2 dH2| C["Products"]
  A -->|Direct dH| C

tip: Draw a simple energy cycle (triangle with arrows) connecting reactants, intermediate and products with the known and unknown ΔH values — this earns the diagram mark.

def: Entropy is a measure of the degree of disorder or randomness of a system; entropy change (ΔS) during a process tells whether disorder increases or decreases.
points: ΔS = qrev/T for a reversible process at temperature T.
Entropy increases when a solid melts, a liquid boils, or a gas is produced (more disorder) — ΔS positive.
Entropy decreases when a gas condenses or a liquid freezes (less disorder) — ΔS negative.
Entropy of a perfectly ordered crystalline solid at 0 K is taken as zero (third law of thermodynamics basis).
Entropy increases when the number of moles of gas increases in a reaction.
ΔS(reaction) = ΣS°(products) - ΣS°(reactants) using standard entropy values.
formula: ΔS = qrev / T     ΔS(rxn) = S(products) - S(reactants)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Solid low entropy"] --> B["Liquid medium entropy"]
  B --> C["Gas high entropy"]
  C --> D["Entropy increases solid to gas"]

example: For melting of ice at 273K, if latent heat = 6008 J/mol, ΔS = q/T = 6008/273 ≈ 22 J/K/mol (positive, as disorder increases).
tip: Relate entropy change directly to the physical state change (solid/liquid/gas) involved — this reasoning is what fetches marks, not just the formula.

def: Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy to determine whether a process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure.
points: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.
ΔG represents the maximum useful work obtainable from a process, excluding work done against pressure-volume changes.
A reaction can be spontaneous even if ΔH is positive, as long as TΔS is large enough and positive.
At equilibrium, ΔG = 0, so ΔH = TΔS, giving the temperature at which the reaction just becomes spontaneous.
Standard Gibbs free energy change ΔG° relates to equilibrium constant K by ΔG° = -RT ln K.
formula: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS     ΔG° = -RT ln K

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Enthalpy change DH"] --> C["Gibbs free energy DG"]
  B["Entropy term T times DS"] --> C
  C --> D["DG = DH minus T DS"]

tip: Keep ΔH in Joules (not kJ) when using ΔS in J/K/mol in the same equation, or convert ΔS to kJ/K/mol — unit mismatch is the top numerical error.

def: Spontaneity criteria use the sign of ΔG to predict whether a process will occur on its own without external help, at constant temperature and pressure.
points: ΔG < 0: the process is spontaneous (occurs on its own in the forward direction).
ΔG > 0: the process is non-spontaneous (will not occur on its own; the reverse process is spontaneous).
ΔG = 0: the system is at equilibrium; no net change occurs.
If ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG is always negative — spontaneous at all temperatures.
If ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0, ΔG is always positive — non-spontaneous at all temperatures.
If signs of ΔH and ΔS are the same (both positive or both negative), spontaneity depends on temperature.
formula: DG<0 spontaneous | DG=0 equilibrium | DG>0 non-spontaneous

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["DG negative"] --> B["Spontaneous"]
  C["DG zero"] --> D["Equilibrium"]
  E["DG positive"] --> F["Non-spontaneous"]

example: Melting of ice above 273K: ΔH is positive (absorbs heat) but ΔS is positive and large enough that TΔS > ΔH, making ΔG negative, so melting is spontaneous above 0°C.
tip: Make a small 4-case table of ΔH and ΔS sign combinations and the resulting spontaneity — this exact table is frequently asked.
